cim: Spinoza and the Thinking Machine: The Philosophy of God, Nature and Artificial Intelligence
cim_eredeti: Spinoza and the Thinking Machine: The Philosophy of God, Nature and Artificial Intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
Amongst the great philosophers of the seventeenth century, few are more relevant to the intellectual revolution represented by artificial intelligence than Baruch Spinoza. This rather solitary Dutch philosopher, who lived between 1632 and 1677, developed a metaphysical system so radically different from the prevailing religious and philosophical orthodoxies of his age that he was expelled from the Jewish community of Amsterdam. His principal work, the Ethics, published posthumously in 1677, proposed nothing less than a comprehensive account of reality, human consciousness, reason, freedom and morality, all derived from a small number of fundamental metaphysical propositions. Almost three and a half centuries later, his ideas offer a remarkably fruitful way of understanding what large language models are, what they might become and why their existence presents such profound philosophical difficulties for our traditional understanding of the human mind.

Spinoza is often regarded as one of the most uncompromising rationalists in the history of Western philosophy. He believed that reality was ultimately intelligible, that everything which happens has a cause and that the apparent distinction between the mental and physical worlds is not quite what we imagine it to be. Human beings are not miraculous exceptions to the natural order, possessing some mysterious power to intervene in a universe otherwise governed by immutable laws. Rather, we are parts of nature, and our thoughts, intentions, desires and decisions form part of the same universal system of causation as the movements of the planets or the growth of plants. This proposition, radical in the seventeenth century, has acquired renewed importance now that machines appear capable of performing activities previously considered exclusive characteristics of human intelligence.

The central question posed by contemporary artificial intelligence is not merely whether machines can produce convincing imitations of human conversation. They plainly can, and with increasing sophistication they can also engage in mathematical reasoning, legal analysis, scientific hypothesis formation and philosophical discussion. The deeper question is whether these activities reveal anything about the nature of thought itself, and whether our habitual distinction between minds and machines rests upon a metaphysical misunderstanding. Spinoza provides a framework for considering these questions without immediately resorting either to the romantic assertion that the human mind possesses an inexplicable spiritual quality or to the equally simplistic assertion that human consciousness is nothing more than a computer programme.

Spinoza's most celebrated and controversial proposition is that there exists only one substance, which he identifies with God or Nature, Deus sive Natura. Everything that exists is a manifestation, or what he calls a mode, of this single underlying reality. Unlike the God of traditional monotheistic religion, Spinoza's God is not a supernatural personality standing outside the universe, issuing commands, performing miracles and periodically rearranging the natural order. God is the infinite, necessarily existing reality within which everything else exists and through whose nature everything else can be understood.

This doctrine is known as substance monism, and it carries an extraordinary implication for contemporary artificial intelligence. If everything that exists is ultimately an expression of one underlying reality, there can be no absolute metaphysical division between human beings and the machines they construct. A human brain and a silicon processor are both configurations of matter governed by physical laws, although they are constituted differently and operate through different causal mechanisms. There is no reason, merely from the fact that one structure is biological and another artificial, to suppose that the former enjoys some privileged status outside the natural order.

This does not establish that artificial intelligence is conscious. Spinoza's metaphysics cannot simply be invoked to confer subjective experience upon a computer, and his understanding of thought differs substantially from our contemporary conception of information processing. Nevertheless, his philosophy challenges a deeply embedded human prejudice: the assumption that the products of human manufacture must necessarily occupy a fundamentally inferior category of existence to their creators. From a Spinozist perspective, the distinction between natural and artificial intelligence is a distinction within nature, not a distinction between nature and something lying outside it.

Thought and extension: two descriptions of the same reality

One of Spinoza's most original arguments concerns the relationship between mind and matter. René Descartes, his philosophical predecessor, had argued that thinking substance and extended substance were fundamentally different kinds of things. This Cartesian dualism left philosophers with an enduring difficulty: how can an immaterial mind interact with a material body? How can something possessing no physical extension cause the movement of a human arm, or how can the impact of a physical object produce the subjective experience of pain?

Spinoza rejected the premise of this problem. Thought and extension, he argued, are two attributes of the same underlying substance, two different ways in which the single reality can be understood. In Proposition VII of Part II of the Ethics, he famously asserted that the order and connection of ideas is the same as the order and connection of things. The mental and physical are not two separate universes mysteriously communicating with one another, but different expressions of the same underlying reality, although neither is simply reducible to the other.

This argument has startling implications when applied to contemporary large language models. A modern artificial neural network consists of an immense mathematical structure, implemented physically through electronic hardware, within which numerical representations are transformed according to learned relationships. What appears to the user as a coherent philosophical argument is, from an engineering perspective, a succession of calculations performed by physical components. Yet the fact that the process can be described mathematically does not settle whether its significance is exhausted by that description.

Indeed, Spinoza might have regarded the attempt to establish an absolute distinction between intelligence and computation as misconceived. Human thinking also has a physical expression in the activities of the brain, although this does not mean that the experience of thinking can be adequately explained merely by describing the electrical behaviour of neurons. His philosophy invites us to consider whether complex artificial systems might possess forms of organisation that deserve to be understood in mental as well as physical terms. It does not prove that they do, because the correspondence between physical processes and thought in his metaphysical system cannot straightforwardly be equated with the relationship between computer hardware and software.

There is a distinction here between having a physical description of a process and possessing a satisfactory philosophical account of what that process accomplishes. A large language model can be described in terms of matrices, weights, probabilities and transformations of numerical representations. But this description alone does not answer whether the system understands the subject matter it discusses, any more than a description of neuronal activity automatically explains the experience of listening to a Beethoven symphony. The difficulty concerns not whether physical processes are involved, but what sorts of explanation are sufficient to account for understanding.
